vignette:
Kaimana was sixty-three years old, a publisher at a mid-sized academic press, married for thirty-four years, and he had not been inside a bar or a restaurant with a liquor license since the night of March 12, 2018. That was the evening he and a close colleague had stopped for a drink at a club in Midtown to celebrate the colleague's promotion. He remembered the beer in his hand, the dim lights, the way the room smelled of spilled whiskey and perfume. And then the noise-not music, but something flat and percussive that he first mistook for a speaker blowing out. He remembered the split second of confusion, the way his friend's face changed, and then the screaming. He had dropped to the floor behind the bar, pressed against a cooler, his face inches from a puddle of amber liquid that had leaked from a broken bottle. He stayed there for what felt like an eternity, listening to the pops and the shouts and the wet sounds he could not name, while the smell of alcohol filled his nose and throat. He survived physically unharmed, but his friend did not.

In the months that followed, Kaimana's memories of that night remained brutally clear. He could close his eyes and see the exact pattern of the bar's tile floor, the angle of the overturned stool, the red smear on a discarded cocktail napkin. The images came in full color and uncompressed, forcing their way into his mind at unpredictable moments-while he was trying to read a manuscript, while he was brushing his teeth, while he was driving to work. He learned to keep his mind busy, to fill the silence with podcasts or talk radio, because any lull invited the pictures back. Waking from a nightmare was the worst: the images would linger for minutes, refusing to dissolve, so that he would lie rigid in the dark, certain he could smell alcohol on his own skin even though he had not had a drink in years.

He stopped seeing friends. The ones who had not been there wanted to talk about it, wanted him to process it, wanted to tell him how brave he was, and the ones who had been there were themselves reminders of the night. He let his phone calls go to voicemail, declined every dinner invitation, stopped showing up at the office happy hour. At his desk he always chose the chair that faced the door and kept his back to the window. He scanned the faces of people entering the lobby, cataloging hands, bags, the shape of a jacket. He could not help it. He was watchful the way a prey animal is watchful, and the vigilance did not switch off when he got home. He felt on guard in his own living room, his own kitchen. Ordinary sounds-the furnace clicking on, a car door slamming outside, his wife's footsteps on the stairs-made him jump, his heart seizing before his mind caught up. He once dropped a stack of proofs when a book slid off the shelf in his study, and he stood there shaking, ashamed.

At work he had grown efficient at avoiding conversation. He took meetings in conference rooms where he could sit with the wall behind him, and he left his office door ajar so he could hear what was happening in the hallway. The publisher who had once been known for his steady, calm presence at editorial meetings now spoke in clipped sentences, his eyes darting. His assistant learned not to approach him from behind. His wife learned not to touch him when he was absorbed in something, because he would flinch and sometimes recoil. She had been patient, but she had also, finally, begun to ask him to talk to someone. He had resisted for years. It was a single moment, he told himself. He had not been hurt. Other people had it worse. But the hypervigilance and the intrusive images had worn grooves into his daily life, and the grooves were getting deeper.

What finally brought him to the clinic was an evening in early autumn when he was alone in the house. His wife was out at a book club-something he would never have allowed her to attend alone before, but he had to let her live, he told himself-and he was reading a page proof when a neighbor's barbecue smoke drifted through the open window. The smell of charcoal and lighter fluid hit him, and suddenly he was back on that tile floor, the alcohol smell flooding his senses, the shouts and pops in his ears. He dropped the manuscript, his hands shaking, and it took him nearly ten minutes to convince himself he was in his own study. He called his wife and asked her to come home early. The next morning he made an appointment.

He is not sure what he hopes for. The idea of talking about that night, of letting the memories surface intentionally, feels dangerous-like opening a door he has spent six years trying to keep shut. But he is tired of sitting with his back to the wall. He is tired of scanning rooms. He is tired of jumping at the click of a lamp. He wants to stop being on guard inside his own home. He wants to be able to smell a glass of wine at dinner without his chest tightening. He wants to feel safe, even if he no longer fully believes safety is possible.
